# Macchajātaka (Ja 75)
**ID:** Ja 75
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Macchajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja75
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Macchajātaka* (Ja 75; PTS J i 329–330) is a short narrative belonging to the Ekanipāta of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Harris; Fausböll 1877]. The story's canonical verse opens with the incipit *Abhitthanaya Pajjunna* ("Pajjunna, thunder!") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The framing tale (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana during a severe drought in the country of Kosala, when the crops withered, ponds dried up, and the Buddha miraculously caused rain to fall [SuttaCentral; Harris; Fausböll 1877].
In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was reborn as the king of the fish in a large pond [SuttaCentral; Harris; UNDV Conference 2009]. When drought struck and the water receded into mud, leaving fish and tortoises helpless prey to predatory crows and hawks, the Bodhisatta was moved by deep compassion for his kin [SuttaCentral; Harris; UNDV Conference 2009]. Rather than merely holding an internal feeling, he made an assertion of his righteous conduct to petition Pajjunna (the rain deity Parjanya) to send rain, thereby restoring the natural order and preserving aquatic life [Harris; UNDV Conference 2009]. In Southeast Asian Buddhist traditions, such as in Cambodia and Thailand, this narrative serves as the prototype for royal and rural rainmaking ceremonies, where monks endure the blazing sun to recite rain-invoking texts beside ritual pits populated by fish and water creatures [Harris].
Neither SuttaCentral nor the automated DharmaNexus analyses record direct textual parallels or cross-language alignments with this entry [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. The text should not be confused with other homonymous stories in the Jātaka collection, such as Ja 34 (opening *Na maṁ sītaṁ na maṁ uṇhaṁ*) or Ja 216 (opening *Na mayaṁ aggi tapati*) [Fausböll 1877; Fausböll 1879].
**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for ja75 — Supplied the canonical title, English translation title, and plot summary of the framing narrative.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus parallel analysis for ja75 — Confirmed the absence of automated cross-linguistic or Pali-internal reuse matches.
- [Fausböll 1877] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 1 (1877) — Provided the Pali incipit and opening commentary of Ja 75, as well as text of Ja 34.
- [Fausböll 1879] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 2 (1879) — Provided text of the homonymous Ja 216.
- [Harris] Ian Harris, Fertility elements in south and southeast Asian Buddhism — Detailed the Bodhisatta's petition to Pajjunna, PTS reference J i 329f, and Southeast Asian rainmaking rituals based on the story.
- [UNDV Conference 2009] Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis, UNDV Conference Volume (2009) — Discussed the environmental and compassionate motifs of the fish king's act of truth in Macchajātaka.
